speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The COVID-19 situation is most likely to last many more months, including the possibility of recurring waves of infection across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must therefore, make contingency plans to safely conduct our next General Election under COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is the responsible thing to do, to robustly plan ahead, to keep our citizens safe while upholding our democracy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They are on top of sections 56A to 56F of the Parliamentary Elections Act, which already contain powers to deal with some disruptive events.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The key provisions in this Bill are in two main parts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The first deals with voters who are subject to movement control orders, that is, COVID-19 stay orders, commonly known as Stay-Home Notice or SHN in short, a COVID-19 Quarantine Order or QO in short, or being on Medical Certificate (MC) because he/she shows Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The second part allows an aspiring candidate to authorise a representative to file his or her nomination paper if the aspiring candidate is unable or unfit to do so because of a COVID-19 QO, SHN, hospitalisation or ill health.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will first cover the clauses, which will allow us to make special arrangements for voters subject to movement control orders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In particular, those on SHN will be allowed to vote outside of their electoral divisions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is because a number of voters, since 10 April, have been required to serve their SHN at designated facilities such as hotels for 14 days to isolate themselves from others and we will continue to issue SHN as part of the strategy to control community transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Their names will be restored to the electoral registers without penalty.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There will be auto-restoration for those on QO and serving their SHN at home, as we have the information for this group.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For those on MC for ARI, they can apply to restore their names to the registers after the election and we will restore them without penalty.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do this to minimise their direct contact with other voters.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is possible because, unlike persons on MC for ARI, those on SHN are already co-located physically in designated facilities thus allowing such arrangements to be rapidly deployed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Polling at the special polling stations will be akin to that at overseas polling stations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Clause 6 requires that a poll and voting at an election involving electors subject to SHN be conducted in the same manner as voting at a polling station in Singapore, with the following modifications: First, instead of the usual voting hours from 8 am to 8 pm, the Returning Officer can set the voting hours at the special polling stations differently, as long as they are at least four hours and end by close of polls at all the other polling stations in Singapore, that is, by 8 pm on Polling Day.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, there can only be one polling agent for each political party, independent candidate or group of independent candidates at each of the special polling stations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The election official at the special polling stations will have to call out the electoral division and polling district code of the voter before issuing a ballot paper, because each special polling station would have voters from many electoral divisions casting their votes there.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If there are no dedicated ballot boxes provided for voting in different electoral divisions at each special polling station, the election officials will have to sort the ballot papers from the opened ballot boxes according to electoral divisions first before starting to count the votes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Under Clause 6(3), the Minister is empowered to make regulations setting out additional modifications to the Parliamentary Elections Act, so as to minimise exposure of the general public or election officials to individuals who may be incubating or infected by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Parliamentary Elections Act requires aspiring candidates to submit their nomination papers in person.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The authorised representative must have the Power of Attorney to authorise him or her to act on behalf of the candidate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The authorised representative will be able to file objections and make amendments to the nomination papers on the candidate’s behalf during the nomination proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The other requirements for successful nomination, such as having the Political Donation Certificate and the required number of subscribers, must still be fulfilled.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Bill does not allow for alternative representation for subscriber, that is, proposers, seconders and assentors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As subscribers can be anyone whose name is in the relevant register of electors, aspiring candidates should find a replacement if any of their subscribers is subject to movement control orders like QO, SHN or MC for ARI, or is having a fever or showing ARI symptoms on the day of nomination.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a democracy, voting is a key responsibility and fundamental right of any citizen that enables them to choose their representatives in the government.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is important that we ensure all citizens get an opportunity to choose who represents them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are some clarifications I would like to seek on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 is not the first coronavirus to land on our shores.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Why make these special arrangements temporary when history sometimes has the nasty habit of repeating itself?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there any minimum number of voters that would warrant the setting up of these special polling stations?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the view of contesting parties participating in the General Elections, having too many polling stations may pose a resource challenge for them to deploy their polling agents to ensure transparency and legitimacy of the voting process.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the voters go against the advice of the Returning Officer and the Director of Medical Services?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the polling agents be allowed to witness the process to ensure transparency?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a democracy, voting is a key responsibility and fundamental right of any citizen that enables them to choose their representatives in the government.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   In a democracy, voting is a key responsibility and fundamental right of every citizen that enables them to choose their representatives in the government.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding my support for this bill, may I ask why these temporary special arrangements are made, even though the coronavirus threat can re-occur in future as we have witnessed before in human history?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): A government has a duty of care to its people, and during their term, they are accountable to the voters who have voted them in.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With or without COVID-19, on the day of the election, voters must have the capacity to hold the ruling party accountable for their actions should they fail to live up to the mandate given, while at the same time choose their representatives in government for the following term.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is the contest for votes amongst political candidates that gives the power back to the citizens to decide on the future of the nation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill ensures that citizens retain this power regardless of the current crisis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister has not yet announced when the impending election will be called and by the Government’s own assessment, the COVID-19 situation in Singapore is not yet at a satisfactory phase.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party has previously called on the Government to be judicious in deciding on the timing of the election, bearing in mind the twin priorities of public health and upholding democratic principles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We note that the recent South Korean election was held at a time where the outbreak showed clear signs of declining cases, underscored by mass community testing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, medical experts here have opined that to be certain that we have turned a corner, a sustained decline in cases to zero or near zero, supported by wide testing, would be needed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we debate this Bill, this is the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the Bill itself, the provisions cover the processes for Nomination Day and Polling Day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 9 modifies Nomination proceedings to cater for the event that a candidate is subject to a quarantine or stay home order, or is hospitalised or ill so as to be medically unfit to attend the Nomination in person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The provision allows the candidate to appoint a representative to file his nomination papers in his stead.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a welcome provision, as it will enable a prospective candidate to still contest the election even if he or she is temporarily unable to attend at the Nomination Centre.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One question that comes to mind is that by the time the candidate needs to utilise this provision, he would already be ill or under a quarantine or stay home order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will he be facilitated to execute the Power of Attorney?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, will a lawyer be allowed access to the candidate to witness the document?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another question relates to who can be a candidate's representative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is provided in clause 9(3) that a representative should be a Singapore citizen who is entitled to vote at the election and duly authorised under a power of attorney.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That being the case, I would like the Government’s confirmation that there is no objection to a representative being a fellow GRC candidate or an assentor or subscriber already present at the Nomination Centre.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to the arrangements as to Polling Day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, voters under Quarantine or Stay Home Orders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 provides that voters who are under quarantine orders or stay home orders are excused from voting and that they cannot leave their designated places of home unless the Returning Officer makes arrangements for them to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the RO does make such arrangements, the voters may then choose to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems to be then that there are two uncertainties here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, it is not clear that the RO will definitely make arrangements for such voters to vote, and second, even if such arrangements are made, voters may choose not to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned about whether this clause will result in significant numbers of people not voting, when they may not be medically ill but simply ordered to be confined as a precaution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Explanatory Statement to the Bill, this provision would also cover those who are on five days' medical leave due to having acute respiratory symptoms earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From what I understand from the South Korean election, voters under quarantine were facilitated to vote, but only after 6.00 pm when the polling booths had closed to the general public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This arrangement protected other voters but also ensured that quarantined voters could vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If there were to be a cluster of infections in a certain area, there could be a significant number of voters for a particular constituency that could fall within this category.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the ELD not able to commit to giving all such voters the opportunity to vote?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 4 to 6 deal with voters who are confined to boarding premises which are not their ordinary residences, such as hotels, apartments and dormitories.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the ELD's proposal to provide special polling stations at or near these premises to facilitate the voters' right to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this, clause 5 states that the Returning Officer (RO) may establish a special polling station, where there are two or more voters form the same constituency in the same boarding premises.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The use of "may" suggests that the RO may decide not to establish such special polling stations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the ELD's intention as to when it will or will not do so?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister also clarify why the Government requires at least two voters from the same constituency to be staying at the same boarding premise, before a special polling station will be set up?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For such voters confined to boarding premises, clause 6(3) states that the Minister may provide for the marking of votes remotely, that is, the voter need not turn up at the special polling station but may mark his vote, for example, in his room and hand his vote securely to the Returning Officer (RO).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There may be a good intention behind this, but it adds a risk to the voting process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 7 thus provides that in such a situation, the usual prohibitions against transporting electors to and from polling stations will not apply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, it is useful to bear in mind the rationale for the prohibition on transporting electors in the first place, to ensure that on Polling day, voters may be casting their votes of their free will without undue influence or pressure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It will be useful if the ELD can share its thinking, so voters know what to expect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How much more is likely to be spent on an election with such additional requirements?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will this be implemented at the polling stations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, past practice shows that voters tend to congregate at the polling stations early in the morning, and by lunchtime the polling stations are quite empty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will voters be advised to spread themselves out this time?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What else can the Elections Department (ELD) share on the practical considerations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the issue of campaigning, Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean had told this House on 25 March that in view of the pandemic, campaign methods will need adjustment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When will the ELD make known the exact changes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, whatever changes are made, it is also critical that these modifications do not result in an escalation of campaign costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Such remote voting technologies might allow us to reduce in-person voting, which will make it easier to protect public health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I also wish to ask why the Bill does not address safe campaigning regulations under COVID-19, which should be defined well in advance of the polls, so that all parties can prepare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Polling may take place during circuit breaker measures, not by design, but due to necessity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Candidates and our campaign regulations will need to be prepared in advance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me discuss the issue of remote electronic voting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since 2001, the Parliamentary Elections Act (PEA) has contained provisions for electronic voting, through Direct-Recording Electronic or DRE voting machines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When the 2001 amendment to the PEA was debated many Members treated DRE voting with caution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Members argued that voters might be unfamiliar with the technology, expressed concerns about maintaining voter secrecy and asked how could DRE voting be proven to be free from electoral abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The passage of 20 years has given many reasons for greater trust in both factors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many Singaporeans now routinely use remote electronic technology to transfer money, pay bills, make investments, file claims in Court and more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And most Singaporeans do not question whether technology can securely determine the identity of the user and record their decision properly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As for trust in the voting process, there are six elected Opposition Members today, most of whom won their seats in a GRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So I do hope the debate on the nature of democracy in Singapore has moved on beyond questioning the voting procedure itself, although I do appreciate as Ms Lim has reminded us that we should always be vigilant to safeguard democracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think we should ask: why not consider provisions for secure remote electronic voting?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To be clear, convenience alone would not be a good reason for remote electronic voting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Voting in public binds Singaporeans together as we exercise our democratic rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But during COVID-19, having a significant fraction of electors choose to use remote electronic voting would greatly reduce crowding at polling stations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Crucially, this would free up polling stations for elderly voters, who are less likely to use remote electronic voting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, there are many cases where electors could have difficulty exercising their right to vote in person, while protecting public health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I wish to ask why the Bill does not address the conduct of campaigns during COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the PEA does not govern campaigning in detail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But nonetheless, the Government could have used this Bill to enact temporary amendments to the PEA or to other Acts to create a legislative framework to govern campaigning during COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am not so worried that there will be a free-for-all in campaigning that puts public health at risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that the ELD will consult with MOH and issue instructions on the conduct of the campaign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, I am asking whether we should do more to ensure that a broad framework to allow for a range of restrictions on campaigning, calibrated to the public health risks, is put into the primary legislation for the duration of COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there are reasons to err on the side of being exhaustive in the primary legislation, where elections are concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The PEA itself goes into detail on voting procedure because it is important that every aspect which might affect the integrity of the vote be subject to as little discretion as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Through this, all candidates are assured that the electoral process reflects the laws agreed and passed by Parliament, rather than the decisions made on the ground by individual officers or the regulations issued by the ELD.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the lack of discretion can be a virtue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The hallmarks of a normal campaign – gathering volunteers, holding rallies, attempting to meet as many electors as possible – all involve significant personal contact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should, therefore, define rules for specific campaign activities which may be allowed as essential, depending on the severity of the COVID-19 outbreak at the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And defining these rules well in advance will allow candidates to prepare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, a good framework would first aim to govern the campaign activities the candidate can engage in, which may include restrictions on places that can be visited, number of electors that can be contacted, rallies and so forth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, to govern the number of persons, other than the candidates, who can assist in physical campaign operations, as each additional person naturally adds to the public health risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, candidates may face difficulties accessing Internet advertising during the campaign, as this also depends on the cooperation of the Internet platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government will address these in the reply, or in subsequent legislation if necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, if anybody had ever doubted the importance of a strong government, I believe that this current pandemic should have ended those doubts.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can you imagine a Singapore with a runaway infection number of critically ill patients without the circuit breaker in force?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can you imagine a Singapore where the Government is too weak to make the tough but necessary choices?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I cannot imagine what the situation would be without all those.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am fortunate and am grateful how we are faring now in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are the far-reaching strict and painful measures that only a democratically elected Government with a strong mandate from the people can enact effectively during an outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A politically weak Government will not have the political capital or legitimacy to do this.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Legitimacy is only conferred with a free and fair election, and only a legitimate Government can get a strong mandate from the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Without the strong mandate from the people, the Government will not be able to make the best possible decisions to steer us out of this crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean has said in Parliament, unless it is a state of emergency, it would be unconstitutional not to hold an election before the date of 14 April 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore, since its founding until now, has not declared a state of emergency and we should not take it lightly to set this precedent.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the Government fails to defend the Constitution, how can it answer to the people who have elected it time after time since our independence in 965?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How are we going to answer to the voters?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Several opposition parties have said that the Government would be most irresponsible if it were to call for a General Election during the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But no one really knows if COVID-19 will end before 14 April 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Of course, I sincerely hope that COVID-19 will be behind us by then.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But even if it is not fully eradicated, it would be most irresponsible of the Government not to call a General Election by 14 April 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we are trying to uphold the Constitution, we also cannot risk a flaring of the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singaporeans from all walks of life have been suffering economically from the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The sacrifices of these people cannot be made in vain.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The real question is how do we do this effectively?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Specifically, we have to explore all the ways to make sure that physical voting is safer, for example, staggered polling times, more polling stations, less contact from sharing objects.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Other than that, we also need to use this opportunity to explore other areas which are not stipulated in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, to use internet technology to enable online voting instead of physical voting.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we allow online voting if the voters log in with their SingPass?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There will always be new issues to address.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, privacy, the secrecy of the votes, cybersecurity and also fraud.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Seniors may also need help in technical areas.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But as with any encounter with new things and new developments, we have to endeavour to try to overcome all the difficulties and challenges in order to move forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the COVID-19 outbreak has taught us one thing, it is that many things that were similarly described as impossible in January this year had in fact been shown to be possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ensuring safe and fair campaigning is as important as ensuring safe and fair polling.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In order to ensure fairness of the election, these boundaries are very important.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We talk about having to choose between liberty and life.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in real life, execution is of the essence.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we should aim for is to allow our voters to exercise their democratic rights safely.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If you fail to plan, you plan to fail.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we make the right decisions and start preparing now, our voters will not need to make a trade-off between democracy and health.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is very easy to say "no", but our responsibility is to find a more effective, safer and win-win solution.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the old adage says, "A sunken ship watches a thousand boats pass by it, a withered tree sees ten thousand saplings blossom beyond it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (As the old continue to wither away, the new will blossom and lead the way.)" Sir, we will be able to find a new way of polling that will adapt to the new information age.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore will definitely rise again from the ashes of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There have been indications that an election is imminent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Electoral Boundary Review Committee released its boundary report in March.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Historically, elections have been called within a month or two after the announcement of the Electoral Boundary Review Committee.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Lee has also not discounted the possibility of a COVID-19 election and said he would judge the situation at hand first.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill at hand is a laudable effort.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am not certain that its current form is truly sufficient to protect the safety of the electorate nor the integrity of our political processes should an early election be called for whilst we are deep in this battle with COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, Mr Speaker, the right to vote forms the foundation of our representative democracy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It concerns me that the Bill in providing for an election in a pandemic excludes a significant segment of the electorate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This, to my mind, inevitably threatens the integrity of our democracy by taking away the voting rights of citizens and, as a consequence, weakens the mandate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What this therefore means is that citizens under quarantine orders face legal repercussions if they attempt to vote.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the case of voters under Stay-Home Notices (SHNs), the Bill stipulates that if at least two individuals residing in one boarding premise exist, the Returning Officer can then establish a special polling station for these voters.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even if we discount those in the dormitories, I think we are still looking at about 15,000.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This number is expected to rise, which gives a sense of the number of Singaporeans who would be prevented from voting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, section 8 of the Bill allows for possible exemption of those who may be unwell or vulnerable to illness or exposure to be discouraged from voting, applying to those Singaporeans who may be first-order contacts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The number of cases in Singapore has exceeded 17,500, when I last checked, with unlinked cases in the community continuing to emerge, indicative of a larger, hidden reservoir of COVID-19 cases in the community that continues to go undetected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If an election is held in a time when we are still grappling with a high risk of community spread, we may be looking at a significant part of the population being discouraged from voting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is an implied right, arising from the various provisions in the Constitution, including Articles 65 and 66," said the Minister for Law in a parliamentary debate in 2009.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Explicitly, section 38(1) of the Parliamentary Elections Act states that the presence of an elector in the register of electors is "conclusive evidence for the purpose of determining whether a person is or is not entitled to vote at the election".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Does the exclusion of voters in this Bill not therefore deprive Singaporeans of this right?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Minister please clarify on the constitutional invalidity of depriving quarantined voters of that right to vote, especially how they have no legal defence if they exit their quarantine holdings to vote?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An election cannot truly be held in good faith if Singaporeans are forced to choose between voting and protecting themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, have we accounted for the thousands of eligible Singaporeans overseas who are excluded because they may not be able to vote at the designated polling stations because of lockdown measures and travel restrictions?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister please clarify if the Bill has been formulated with these concerns in mind and if not, how does the Government intend to rectify this potential loss of more voters?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, I cannot help but sincerely question just how strong and fresh of a mandate the new government can marshall in a COVID-19 General Election where there are such significant parts of the electorate excluded from voting by law, by illness, by fear and by choice, which would most certainly result in substantially lower voter turnout.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: MHA, Cyber Security Agency and Elections Department have issued advisories to political parties on the threat of foreign interference.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Under the guidelines of the advisories issued, political parties are expected to not only shore up their digital literacy but also beef up their existing IT infrastructure and security.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Not all political parties will have the necessary resources to ensure full and adequate compliance with the advisories and this is especially concerning given that a COVID-19 election will likely heavily depend on social media and other online platforms for campaigning to replace rallies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some believe that rallies contribute to the leveling of the playing field, and give fair opportunity for each political party to offer their pitch.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To have an election without rallies would be disadvantageous to parties with less resources.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill does not seem to have any provisions for fair campaigning.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, Mr Speaker, apart from the integrity of the mandate and democratic processes, we cannot discount the possibility that holding an election any time soon will increase the risk of transmission again.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that measures can be taken to ensure higher sanitary standards in voting booths throughout voting day.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must not forget that all it takes are a few minor lapses to trigger another dangerous bout of contagion.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Just looking at how quickly the virus spreads in weeks with 200,000 workers across different dormitories should alarm us to what we would be risking to allow large hordes of people to come together at the polling stations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some may urge us to look at the example of South Korea to suggest that elections can still be successfully held without risk to public health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: South Korea, however, had managed to stem their flow of infections before they held their election.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Besides, we do not even know if the South Korean elections will lead to a relapse in infections, given the 14-day incubation period.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Already, there are worrying trends that the virus is more devious and more complicated than previously thought.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: No one can say for sure how long this public health crisis will last until it is actually over.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I do therefore humbly urge the Minister to direct the energies and resources of this Government – which still has a full year mandate ahead of it – to be focused on resolving the crisis and safeguarding the physical and mental health of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And not to burden the severely-stretched public service further with an early election, particularly with the colossal inter-agency efforts to resolve the migrant worker crisis that are ongoing and will be needed beyond COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If not, we may consider holding an election at that time according to the terms of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Alternatively, if the situation in fact worsens in a way that will still hamper a fair election, this House may have to consider passing a constitutional amendment to extend the deadline for an election.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If we are to pass this Bill today, we must make sure that the Bill is comprehensive in ensuring both the safety of the electorate, maximum suffrage and fair campaigning.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will also help to quell sentiments on the ground that an early election is being exercised for political expediency, avoiding an undue erosion of public trust.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Any yes that is given without the ability to safely say no is never a true choice.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And therefore not the kind of vote or mandate we want the new government to be built upon, especially to lead us in a post-COVID world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am supportive of planning for all contingencies to enable as many eligible Singaporean voters to cast their votes as possible in a General Election.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the end of the day, we do not want a situation where we are forcing Singaporeans to choose between their right to vote and their health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to have plans and back-up plans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to have resources to ensure that we can implement our plans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also should ensure our message is clear that those who are not well should stay home and that those who are well can safely vote because we have taken all necessary precautions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can try to predict but it is difficult to say for certain how the number of infections will unfold.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the event that the number of people subject to COVID-19 Stay Order Regulations and living at boarding premises increase significantly, more special polling stations will be required.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the measures taken to ensure that we have sufficient resources to operate special polling stations and, if necessary, to transport electors such that every elector subject to the COVID-19 Stay Order Regulations and living at boarding premises will have access to a special polling station?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what public health and safety measures will be implemented at special polling stations to prevent disease transmission?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The explanatory note elaborates that such an elector may remain in his or her room at the boarding premises, be delivered the ballot paper to mark secretly, and return it using a secure method to the Returning Officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a very significant departure from in person voting at polling stations and is not subject to the usual protective measures at polling stations to ensure the secrecy of votes such as the presence of polling agents, the sealing of ballot boxes and the supervision of a presiding officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Where votes are collected from individual electors’ rooms, as opposed to where votes are cast at a single location, there are many more points where the secrecy of the vote may be undermined.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are measures that can be taken to ensure the secrecy and integrity of the vote and the Explanatory Note states that the regulations need to be consistent with principles such as secrecy of the vote and one-person-one-vote.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what are some of the protective measures that may be introduced in regulations if it is necessary for an elector to vote from his or her room?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, as early as November 2018, the Elections Department (ELD) announced new technology and processes to be used at the next elections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include counting machines, electronic registration, and self-inking pens.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ELD announced in November 2019 that it would hold roadshows ahead of the next General Election to familiarise voters with the new equipment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ELD also announced that it will organise sessions for political party representatives to try out the new digital services and provide feedback.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Training would clearly also need to be carried out for counting agents who will have to operate the counting machines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what measures will be implemented to ensure that voters, polling agents, and counting agents can be familiarised with these new initiatives to ensure smooth roll out on polling day itself?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will training be conducted if on-site sessions cannot be conducted, for example during circuit breaker periods?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is likely that the voting process will be slower because of the additional safety measures taken, the new technology used and the potential need to transport electors to special polling stations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what plans there are to address any potential delays in the polling process that might affect electors’ ability to vote before the close of the poll on Polling Day, whether at a regular polling station or a special polling station?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these cities are currently and may in the future have high rates of disease transmissions and may be in varying states of lockdown.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While overseas electors may form a small proportion of the voters, they too are citizens of Singapore and it is important to preserve their right to vote as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what the COVID-19 special arrangement plans are in relation to overseas voters?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will address the points specific to this Bill first before I cover the other points.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Anthea Ong expressed her concern that the Bill deprives certain voters of their right to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Rather, the special arrangements in this Bill will in fact allow more voters to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Under the Infectious Diseases Act, a voter on QO, or SHN cannot leave his or her place of isolation or accommodation without the permission of the Director of Medical Services.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, this Bill enables special arrangements to be made to allow those on SHN staying at designated facilities to vote under special arrangements that will minimise their contact with other voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Thus, the arrangements afforded by this Bill should allay concerns among the wider voting population who might otherwise be dissuaded from voting because of in-person voting by those under SHN.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To use Ms Ong’s own words, Singaporeans should not have to choose between voting and protecting themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Ms Sylvia Lim has noted, the Bill merely recognises that voters who are under QO or an SHN at home have a legitimate reason for not voting because of the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To Ms Lim’s question, the Elections Department will consult MOH and MHA nearer the election date to assess if the public health and security risks of allowing these two categories of voters to leave their homes and making special arrangements for them to vote in-person at polling stations can be managed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked about clause 8 which provides for the Returning Officer and the Director of Medical Services to advise voters who are unwell to be socially responsible and not turn up to vote at the polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Public health issues still need to be addressed even during an election and our officials should not be prevented from doing so because of the offence that is in section 81(1) of the Parliamentary Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would add that this clause only applies to public advisories for the awareness of voters in general and is not directed at any particular voter or voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Voters will be required to comply with the directives of the Returning Officer or the Director of Medical Services.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is to ensure the safety of others and the Election Officers will explain this to the voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the powers vested in the Minister to make regulations allowing voters subject to COVID-19 stay orders to vote without leaving their boarding premises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The process, if we need to do this, will include extra steps that ensure that the correct voter receives an authentic ballot paper, remind him or her to vote freely and in secret, and that ensures the secure return of his or her marked ballot in secret for counting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also ensure there is transparency as candidates, independent or representing a political party, and their polling agents can be present to observe the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zainal Sapari highlighted the potential resource challenges for candidates and political parties if there are too many special polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Just to give a bit of context, we have over 800 polling stations around the island.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would also like to assure Assoc Prof Walter Theseira and Ms Sylvia Lim that the intention is to enable every voter serving SHN at designated facilities to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about the rationale for requiring at least two or more voters to be from the same constituency before setting up a special polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is to address concerns on the secrecy of the vote where there is a lone SHN voter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In such a case, the Bill provides the flexibility of transporting the lone SHN voter, together with others, to a larger special polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If this is necessary, the Elections Department will put in place the necessary safeguards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would add that the offences of treating, undue influence and bribery in the Parliamentary Elections Act still apply in such a situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let me assure Members that unless the number of SHN voters spikes, the Elections Department's preference is to conduct polling within the designated facilities rather than transporting the voters to special polling stations outside.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim's questions pertaining to the Power of Attorney to be executed by an aspiring candidate who is unable or unfit to file his nomination papers in person, the aspiring candidate can engage a lawyer to prepare the Power of Attorney to expressly authorise the representative to represent and act on behalf of the aspiring candidate at nomination proceedings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This must include an authorisation to submit nomination papers and raise objections to the nomination papers of other candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Bill also does not prevent a GRC candidate or an assentor of the group from doubling up as a representative of another aspiring candidate of the GRC who happens to be unwell as long as he is in possession of the required Power of Attorney.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In drawing up these measures, the Elections Department will abide by the prevailing advisories issued by MOH for health, and MHA for security.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Elections Department is also studying the experiences of countries that have held elections under pandemics, such as South Korea.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the case of South Korea, they implemented precautionary measures, such as temperature screening, safe distancing and requiring voters to wear masks and plastic gloves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another useful observation from the South Korean elections is the wide use of collaterals, such as videos and infographics, to assure voters of the precautionary measures being put in place.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a result, they had a record turnout at the elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The South Korean health authority also recently concluded that there were no local transmission cases arising from the elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond the best practices from South Korea, the Elections Department will also consider Mr Ong Teng Koon's suggestions to increase the number of polling stations and even out the flow of voters across polling hours.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is something that the ELD has started studying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have not implemented online voting as it is difficult to prevent impersonation and ensure voting secrecy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even with SingPass, we do not know for sure if the vote is cast by the person himself or by another person who is assisting him.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For a voter to be sure that his online vote is accurately recorded for audit purpose, present-day IT verification systems will require the system to also retain information on the voter's choice, which will compromise voting secrecy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In addition, there are system reliability issues and security risks, such as vulnerability to hacking and cyber-attacks.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not possible to have polling agents present during online voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira raised a very philosophical point, which is this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have two considerations for the voting process – first, the verification of the voter's identity; second, voting secrecy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, this is fundamentally different from a bank transaction.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A bank transaction verifies the person's transacting identity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, there is an audit trail to allow any dispute to be settled thereafter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a voting situation, it is precisely quite different.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These reasons were highlighted in an article in the 28 April issue of The Economist on why online voting is not the way to hold elections during a pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Louis Ng asked about the Singaporean voters overseas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want Singaporeans who have registered to vote overseas to be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we must also recognise that the COVID-19 situation has affected many cities around the world to different extents and we do not know how it will evolve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a decision that will not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Returning Officer will assess and monitor the situation for each overseas polling station after the writ of election is issued before making any such decision.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on the issue of campaigning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Ong Teng Koon and Assoc Prof Theseira asked about campaigning under the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is outside the scope of the Bill as laid out in its long title.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will just briefly say that the Elections Department will share the guidelines for campaigning in due course, taking into account the COVID-19 situation then.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the Parliamentary Elections Act and its subsidiary legislation cover only some aspects of campaigning like the regulation of election advertising, with rallies and walkabouts covered under the Public Order Act, the Elections Department's practice has been to issue an advisory on campaigning guidelines, together with other relevant authorities like the Police and MHA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Elections Department will also work with MOH on the health and safety aspects of campaigning before issuing its advisory.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will be done with sufficient time for political parties and aspiring candidates to prepare.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Again, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira raised a philosophical point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What are the parts that should go into the Rules and what are the parts that should go into the subsidiary legislation or Regulations?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In general, our philosophy must be this – for those things that are conducted in a defined, structured environment, the fewer the variables, the more we are able to write it down in clear rules, and we should do that upfront.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those activities that are conducted in less structured environments, where things are evolving rapidly, then, certainly, not everything can be written upfront and whatever rules that are going to be made for those activities, including campaigning activities, will have to take into consideration the prevailing health and security considerations by MOH and MHA respectively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the reason why the Bill is structured in this way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For things that are conducted in the polling station, where it is a structured environment, we will try to be as clear, as defined, and to let people know as early as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those things like campaigning, which is conducted in a less structured environment, which is more subject to the evolving health and security considerations, not all of that can be written down prior, and not all of them may need to be written down because then that will circumscribe the actions that may be possible in due course.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the philosophy behind why the Bill is structured in this way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, let me address Mr Zainal Sapari's point about why the arrangements are temporary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I agree with Mr Zainal Sapari that if there are provisions which are relevant to future elections, we will include these provisions when we next amend the Parliamentary Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on the issue of the timing of the election, which is not a part of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Ong Teng Koon commented on the timing of the General Election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ideally, we would all like to conduct elections in normal conditions but it is uncertain when the COVID-19 situation will stabilise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, as South Korea has shown, holding an election under COVID-19 is possible, but there must be adequate precautionary measures in place to safeguard the well-being of voters, candidates and officials, and it will be prudent and responsible for us to make those necessary contingency plans ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a few short months, the way we live, work and interact with others has changed drastically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we cannot plan on the basis that it will.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, we need to plan ahead and put in the necessary measures so that we can hold elections safely even under the new and evolving COVID-19 norms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This Bill allows the Elections Department to implement temporary arrangements to ensure the safety of voters, candidates and election officials should the next General Election take place under the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the responsible thing to do – to consider the prevailing circumstances and plan as robustly as possible – so that we can take care of the well-being of Singaporeans while upholding democracy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I beg to move.      .
